For friction and mass the per-object gain over the free material table is bounded by e1 at ~0.8 mm of 2.6 mm, an increment no robot pipeline would act on, and the robot-transfer evidence that would make it a CoRL/RSS paper is deferred to an unsecured partnership. It does not address the user's scale ask at all. What survives is the 240 fps measurement protocol as a dataset and an engine-portability validation of exported parameters -- reframed that way, with an in-sim SIMPLER ranking experiment replacing the robot partnership, it becomes an actionable and falsifiable contribution; as a per-object twin with a differentiable headline it is Galileo with a better camera.

proposals.title: HELD-OUT: a real-motion benchmark for parameter-assignment pipelines, with a measured material atlas (with uncertainty) as the reference assignment layer
proposals.thesis: Every sim-ready pipeline in the landscape (PhysX-3D/Anything/Omni, UniPhysGen, EmbodiedGen V2, ManiTwin, UrbanVerse, BEHAVIOR-1K, SimReady, SIMPLER) assigns mass and friction from a VLM or a lookup and scores against its own annotations, a VLM judge, product listings or static meter readings; the one test that matters -- does a real object the pipeline never fitted move as predicted -- has never been published, and GAUGE (the only measured-trajectory benchmark) tests engines fed measured values, never assignment. We turn the project's held-out protocol (70 real objects, 359 trials, a floor from repeat trials, invariant checks) into a benchmark that scores assignment routes -- including the released generators PhysX-Anything and UniPhysGen and the LLM routes those catalogues use -- and ship the measured per-material table with uncertainty as the drop-in replacement for the VLM number.
proposals.what_we_build: (1) Benchmark data: Physics 101 ramp footage already tracked by our pipeline (1,968 raw clips at 10/20 deg; 643 classified slide/roll/stay; 101 objects with measured mass and volume and a photo each), split leave-one-object-out, with a per-object noise floor from that object's own repeat trials (the 'oracle' row, 1.8 mm median / 6.2 mm p90). (2) A scorer: trajectory RMS with only release time and offset aligned (never acceleration), stays/slides outcome accuracy at both angles, mass within-25% and median factor; each route is allowed exactly one global 'surface anchor' constant fitted on the training folds (our pair rule mu_pair = sqrt(mu_obj * mu_board) needs it, and so does mapping any pipeline's friction convention), then scored on held-out objects. (3) Routes: oracle, measured table (ours), LLM-name + table (the 80%-accurate naming step), LLM direct number (Claude Opus 5.5 / GPT-6 / Gemini 3.1), VLM friction-RANGE midpoint and DR-expectation (the EmbodiedGen/ManiTwin/UrbanVerse convention), engineering-handbook table (the SimReady artist convention), PhysX-Anything (single photo -> mesh + density -> mass via measured volume), and the chain PhysX-Anything mesh -> UniPhysGen (released 1.7B checkpoints; outputs part friction, density, object mass), which is how a real pipeline would run from one photo. (4) A rule-1 sensitivity audit of the benchmark itself: per held-out object, score as a function of the assigned mu over [0.05, 0.6], giving the identifiability window of the 20 deg ramp (only mu < tan 20 deg = 0.36 slides; 3 of 15 materials never slide). (5) The atlas v1: material -> (mu_pair vs board, rho_eff by build: areal / solid / shell, IQR, n, angle range), exported as a USD PhysicsMaterial / MJCF JSON whose IQR is a MEASURED domain-randomisation range, plus a coverage number: the fraction of PhysXNet (26K objects, open-text material strings) and UniPhys-40K parts whose material maps to a measured row. (6) A phone-ramp extension at 30-40 deg to lift the never-sliding classes and ~10 catalogue materials with no row (paper/books, leather, glass, glazed ceramic, PLA/ABS prints, painted metal, fabric-covered).
proposals.builds_on_our_assets: scripts/e1_heldout.py (routes, LOO-object scoring, LLM cache, mass test) is the benchmark core and runs today; scripts/p1_ramp_friction.py and p2_ramp_all.py (CoTracker3 at the 19 px grid, slide/roll/stay classification, 643 clips, two-angle invariant, camera-scale invariant 1633-1724 px/m); scripts/p4_sim_loop.py (Newton reproduces the real slides to 0.4-1.0 mm RMS, so the forward model is validated on exactly these clips); scripts/p5_transfer.py (pair-friction rule factorised on real data, the single stated anchor body mu = mu_pair^2 / 0.45, areal/solid/shell mass transfer, cd_for_restitution); docs/results/p101_density.json (15 effective densities with n/min/max); scripts/f14_llm_outcomes.py and the Letsur gateway (three LLMs); src/data/assets.MASS_MODEL and MeshProbeScene(mass_model=) with textbook-checked CoM/inertia; src/sim/rigs.py apply_tilt_rig; the 13 assets for the re-parameterisation demo. The simulator is used FORWARD only.
proposals.differentiable_physics_role: Gradients buy little here, and the proposal should say so. Scoring is a forward simulation of a one-parameter sliding law, and the per-clip oracle fit is a 31-point mu grid (p4) that is already exact; the only place a tape could enter is a batched joint fit of (mu, t0, s0) per clip with a Jacobian-based error bar, which is convenience, not capability. This paper would be the same paper on a non-differentiable engine; what matters is that the contact model is VALIDATED against real motion (p4), not that it is differentiable. The tape only becomes load-bearing if the benchmark later adds the drop/topple observables (Proposal 2), where the per-clip inversion is 3-6 dimensional.
proposals.scale_claim: 'Beyond rooms' is the wrong axis for this proposal: a physical parameter belongs to a material, not a scene, so what must scale is the table and the protocol, not a measurement per object or per room. Concretely: 101 objects / 15 materials / 643 classified clips at two angles now; +~10 materials x 5 objects x 5 trials x 2 angles (~500 clips) from the phone ramp; the scale metric is CATALOGUE COVERAGE -- the share of PhysXNet's 26K objects and UniPhys-40K's 400K parts (and, by their published vocabularies, ManiTwin-100K / UrbanVerse-100K) whose material string maps to a measured row, targeted at >= 60% of rigid parts by count after the extension. A 100k-asset urban catalogue consumes the same table at zero marginal cost; nothing per-object has to scale, and that is the point.
proposals.practicality: Users: (1) authors of sim-ready generators and catalogues get the only score on real held-out motion that exists, with a noise floor, per-route failure modes and a pre-registered test; (2) catalogue builders (SimReady, BEHAVIOR-1K/OmniGibson, MolmoSpaces, UrbanVerse, SIMPLER-style evaluation suites) replace 'GPT-4 or Google search' density and 'common material' friction with the atlas JSON + USD/MJCF writer, and replace the guessed DR range (friction 0.1-1.0 in locomotion practice) with the measured within-material IQR (0.01-0.05 wide in Physics 101); (3) our own 13 assets are re-parameterised through p5 and the shift in simulated outcomes (slide/stay, slide distance) between VLM numbers and the atlas is reported. Honest limit: with no robot we cannot show that better object parameters change policy transfer -- SIMPLER's <= 15% sensitivity and the Push-T MPC finding ('mass and friction yield no stable adaptation signal') leave that open, and the paper must say so rather than claim it. On its own this is a benchmark + dataset paper; it becomes a system contribution only with the atlas wired as an assignment layer and the coverage number reported.
proposals.novelty_argument: All six scouts converge on the same gap: no pipeline validates assigned mass/friction against the real motion of held-out objects, and no measurement-grounded benchmark scores assignment (GAUGE scores engines fed measured values; PhysVid, EKFPhys and IRIS score estimators on the objects they measured; PhysX-Bench and UniPhys-Bench score against VLM/human annotations). Our e1 is the only held-out-object transfer result and it is unpublished. What is different from Galileo / Physics 101 (same data): the held-out-object protocol, repeat-trial floors, invariant checks, a 2026 engine validated to 1 mm on these clips, and the scoring of 2025-26 pipelines. What is NOT new, stated plainly: the footage is Physics 101 (2016), not new capture; the ramp's identifiability window is narrow (mu 0.1-0.36 at 20 deg); the e1 numbers themselves already exist. The novelty is the protocol, the first real-motion score of released sim-ready generators, and the measured-uncertainty atlas; the user's 'reinventing the wheel' worry is answered by the pre-registered kill test -- if a released generator already matches the table, we say so and stop.
nearest_prior_work: GAUGE (arXiv 2608.05948): ~1,560 mocap trials with measured mu/e fed INTO Isaac/Genesis/Newton -- validates engines, never an assignment route; our benchmark asks the other question and uses a 2016 dataset with 101 objects instead of 3 rigid materials

PhysVid / Inferring Dynamic Physical Properties (arXiv 2510.02311): dynamometer-measured mu for 5 objects x 6 surfaces, estimators scored by Pearson on the same objects; no held-out transfer, no re-simulation
EKFPhys (arXiv 2309.15703): the only closed-loop estimator check (4 YCB objects, mocap mu); per-object, not transfer
Galileo (NeurIPS 2015) / Physics 101 (BMVC 2016): same footage, outcome-prediction evaluation, 2015 engine; no held-out-object parameter test
PhysX-Omni / PhysX-Bench (2605.21572) and UniPhys-Bench (2607.13586): the generators' own benchmarks score against VLM/human labels or VLM-judged simulation videos
SIMPLER (arXiv 2405.05941): object physics from 'GPT-4 or Google search'; ablation shows evaluation insensitive to them -- the open 'does it matter' question we cannot close without a robot
Our e1 (scripts/e1_heldout.py, docs/results/e1_heldout.json): 70 objects, 359 trials, material 2.6 mm vs oracle 1.8 mm vs LLM number 7.5 mm (p = 1e-7)
first_90_days: Weeks 1-2: run PhysX-Anything (released code + HF weights, single-image) on the 101 Physics 101 photos; chain its mesh into UniPhysGen (released 1.7B checkpoints) for friction/density/mass; score both through e1 with one global anchor fitted on train folds; add GPT-6 / Gemini direct-number, VLM-range-midpoint and handbook-table routes via the gateway. Output: the first-experiment numbers.

Weeks 2-3: rule-1 audit of the benchmark: per held-out object, RMS vs assigned mu over [0.05, 0.6]; identifiability window; bootstrap CIs and paired sign tests for every route pair; report which objects can rank routes and which carry only the one-bit outcome.

Weeks 3-5: coverage: normalise PhysXNet and UniPhys-40K material strings to atlas rows with the LLM naming step (its 80% accuracy is itself a benchmark row); report % parts covered and the ranked list of uncovered materials, which becomes the capture list.

Weeks 5-8: phone ramp at 30 and 40 deg on a known board (60 fps suffices for sliding): foam / rubber / hollow-rubber stand-ins plus the top-10 uncovered materials, 5 objects x 5 trials x 2 angles; the two-angle agreement (rule 1b) and the camera-scale invariant are the admission tests; new anchor stated once.

Weeks 8-10: freeze atlas v1 (mu_pair, rho_eff by build, IQR, n, angle range) + USD PhysicsMaterial / MJCF writer; re-parameterise the 13 project assets and a 50-asset PhysXNet sample; report the outcome shift (slide/stay at 20 deg, slide distance) between VLM numbers and atlas values.
Weeks 10-13: package split files, scorer, routes, floors and the sensitivity audit; write up with the pre-registered kill-test result reported whichever way it went.
proposals.first_experiment: PhysX-Anything on the 101 object photos -> density x measured volume vs measured mass: within-25% fraction and median factor (to beat: build-aware table 69% / x1.11, LLM guess 46% / x1.30); PhysX-Anything mesh -> UniPhysGen friction through the e1 scorer -> held-out trajectory RMS median / p90 over 359 trials and stays/slides accuracy over 198 cases (to beat: table 2.6 / 12.4 mm and 94%; LLM number 7.5 / 44.9 mm and 85%; dataset-wide median 4.4 mm). Two weeks, one A6000, no new capture.
proposals.kill_test: Pre-registered now. (1) The premise ('a measured table beats every assignment route on held-out real motion') is dead if any released generator or VLM route matches the table within the floor: paired sign test vs the table with p > 0.05 AND median RMS within 0.5 mm of 2.6 mm AND mass within-25% >= 65%. Then the catalogues already carry the numbers, we publish that, and the atlas is not built. (2) Rule 1 for the benchmark itself: the score must respond to the assigned parameter beyond the repeat floor -- per held-out object, RMS at (material median +/- 0.05) must exceed the oracle p90 (6.2 mm) for >= 40 of the 70 sliding objects; objects that fail carry only the one-bit outcome and cannot rank routes. (3) Rule 1 for every added data source (phone ramp): admitted only if its two-angle mu agree within the within-object IQR and the between-material spread exceeds 3x the within-object repeat spread.
proposals.resources: One shared A6000 for PhysX-Anything (Qwen2.5-VL-scale) and UniPhysGen (1.7B) inference, hours in total; ~300 LLM-gateway calls; CPU for scoring; Newton forward sims (31 mu x 70 objects) are minutes. Phone ramp: a phone, tripod, a wooden board, ~50 household objects, kitchen scale, 2-3 capture days. No robot, no mocap. Physics 101 (4.5 GB) is on disk.
proposals.biggest_risk: The 20 deg ramp's identifiability window: only mu in [0.1, 0.36] slides, so generators that emit a generic ~0.4 (what f14 measured for LLMs) all score 'stays' and the benchmark reports a uniform failure without ranking them; the 30-40 deg phone ramp fixes this but changes the surface and needs its own anchor and invariants. Second: 7 cm cubes and poles are off the generators' training distribution (furniture-scale assets), which their authors may call unfair -- mitigated by reporting per-route failure modes and per-material breakdowns rather than one leaderboard, and by stating the distribution mismatch. Third: a one-constant anchor per route can hide a convention mismatch (PhysX static/dynamic friction vs our pair mu); the audit must show the anchor is a scale, not a fit.
proposals.expected_headline_result: Expected if everything works: on 70 held-out real objects (359 slides, 198 stay/slide cases) a 15-material table measured from real motion predicts the slides of objects it never saw to 2.6 mm median against a 1.8 mm repeat-trial floor, while the friction and density assigned by two released sim-ready generators and three LLMs land at 5-8 mm and under 50% mass-within-25% -- no better than a dataset-wide median -- the first real-motion score of sim-ready parameter assignment, released with the atlas and its measured uncertainty.

evidence: Physics 101 (Wu et al., BMVC 2016, https://bmva-archive.org.uk/bmvc/2016/papers/paper039/paper039.pdf) ALREADY runs a held-out-OBJECT protocol on this exact footage: 'Split by object: we randomly choose 95% of the objects. We use them as training data and the others as test data ... the most difficult setting as it requires the model to generalize to objects that it has never seen before.' Table 2a reports held-out-object outcome prediction (moving distance r=0.33, bounce height r=0.23, float 84%) against a uniform baseline. The proposal's 'no held-out-object parameter test' for Physics 101 is therefore wrong; what is new is the scoring (mm trajectory RMS via a validated engine, repeat-trial floors, invariants) and the subjects scored, not the split. (Primary source, read locally.)

Galileo (Wu et al., NeurIPS 2015, https://people.csail.mit.edu/billf/publications/5780-galileo-...pdf) already performs the proposal's stays/slides transfer test on the same data: 'predict whether the object will slide down the surface' at 10 deg from a 20 deg video, 50 objects, Bullet engine, model and humans at chance (Galileo vs truth r=0.20). The proposal's 94% on 198 cases would be a real improvement, but the test design is not new. (Primary source, read locally.)

PhysVid / 'Inferring Dynamic Physical Properties from Video Foundation Models' (arXiv 2510.02311, https://arxiv.org/html/2510.02311): the proposal says 'no held-out transfer'; the paper explicitly holds out BOTH objects and surfaces (train: paper box, metal pencil box, wooden box on red towel/wooden table/cardboard; test: plastic disk, LEGO brick on gray towel/kitchen paper/tablecloth), dynamometer ground truth, Pearson + ROC-AUC. Correct part of the characterisation: no re-simulation against real trajectories.

EKFPhys (arXiv 2309.15703, https://arxiv.org/html/2309.15703): real ground-truth friction obtained by the SAME inclined-plane method the project uses ('tilt [the table] ... let it slide 10 times ... mu = tan(alpha) - a/g'), 4 YCB objects x 5 sequences; reports estimate-vs-measured error (median 0.025), NOT a closed-loop re-simulation check as the proposal claims ('the only closed-loop estimator check') -- medium confidence, last 18k chars of the HTML unread.

Kaedim 'Measuring Asset and Scene Reconstruction Effects in Real-to-Sim Robot Evaluation' (arXiv 2610.00731, https://arxiv.org/html/2610.00731v1) + HF dataset projectsim/yam-real-to-sim-assets (16 sim-ready objects, CC BY 4.0, released ~1 week ago): the proposed 'material class -> per-class table' assignment layer is already a deployed convention ('static and dynamic friction are taken from a per-class table keyed on that class'; VLM assigns class, mass, restitution) and is already validated against real robot trials at the policy-score level (Pearson r 0.90 authored vs 0.51 default; mean score error 6.97 vs 17.54 pp). It does NOT validate per-object motion or measured values -- the paper itself states 'object physics ... is left at engine defaults or estimated by a model without validation against measurement' -- which supports the proposal's gap, but the 'does it matter for robot evaluation' question the proposal calls fully open is partially (confoundedly) answered here and must be cited.

GAUGE (arXiv 2608.05948, https://arxiv.org/html/2608.05948): fairly characterised. Rigid track = 3 materials (wood, plastic, metal), 8 task families, 180 Hz mocap, 20 repeats; friction by inclined plane, restitution by air-bearing rail; engines (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) 'set from the GAUGE calibrations'; no VLM/LLM/lookup assignment route evaluated; no per-material uncertainty table confirmed as released; world-model track feeds measured coefficients INTO the prompt and checks law-consistency of generated video.

PhysX-Anything (arXiv 2511.13648, https://arxiv.org/html/2511.13648v1) and UniPhysGen/UniPhys-Bench (arXiv 2607.13586, https://arxiv.org/html/2607.13586): fairly characterised. UniPhys ground truth = 'GPT-5 ... to infer structured physical priors' + manual verification + simulation-consistency filtering; metrics ALDE/MAE/MnRE against those labels; validation is 'qualitatively ... in physics simulation (Isaac Sim)'. PhysX-Anything validates only in 'a MuJoCo-style simulator'. No real-motion validation in either. PhysX-Bench (arXiv 2605.21572) scores with Qwen3.5-122B-A10B as judge.

Held-out mass-from-photo evaluation is well-trodden: NeRF2Physics (arXiv 2404.04242), VoMP (arXiv 2510.22975), PhysVGGT (arXiv 2609.18920), SiPhy (arXiv 2607.22355) all score mass on ABO-500 ('100 held-out objects with catalogue-measured ground-truth weight') and friction/hardness on NeRF2Physics' 13-scene measured set. NeRF2Physics is itself an 'LLM proposes material -> lookup' route scored against measured mu, so 'LLM-name + table' as a ROUTE exists; scoring it on re-simulated motion does not.

No measured per-material friction/density atlas with uncertainty for rigid household materials, exported for simulators, was found for 2023-2026 (closest: PhysVid 5x6 dynamometer table, NeRF2Physics 13 scenes, GAUGE 3 materials, a soft-robotics COF database in Meccanica 2023 s11012-023-01719-5 -- paywalled, not verified). Low-medium confidence: the shared web-search budget was exhausted after ~20 queries, so coverage of 2026 preprints is incomplete.

Other near neighbours checked and found NOT to score assignment against held-out real motion: Scalable Real2Sim (arXiv 2503.00370: robot-measured mass 1.34% error, 'qualitative' rollouts only); Phys2Real (arXiv 2510.11689: 2 objects, VLM prior + interaction); Real2Sim via Active Perception (arXiv 2601.08454: robot measures mass/friction, no VLM-vs-measured table); PhyPush (arXiv 2605.26284: estimator, unseen objects, no re-sim); ExPhy (arXiv 2608.20009: fully synthetic); ViTacPhys (arXiv 2608.21355: held-out-category mass/friction CLASSES, no motion re-sim); Asset2Sim (arXiv 2605.19136: articulated, simulator-feedback only); DiagGen (arXiv 2609.23103: deformables, sim diagnostics only); JBI Physics-Fidelity benchmark (physicalai-bmi.org: analytic + SO-101 arm conservation probes, no object-property assignment).
verdicts.surviving_form: Drop the headline 'has never been published' and the 'first held-out-object test on this data' framing: Physics 101 (2016) already evaluates split-by-object property estimation and outcome prediction, and Galileo already runs the 10-deg-from-20-deg stays/slides transfer on 50 of these objects. What survives, and is still unfound in the 2023-2026 literature: (1) a RE-SIMULATION-scored benchmark (mm trajectory RMS through an engine validated to <1 mm on these clips, repeat-trial noise floor, invariant admission tests, rule-1 sensitivity audit) of parameter-ASSIGNMENT routes rather than estimators -- released sim-ready generators (PhysX-Anything, UniPhysGen), LLM direct-number routes, and the per-class-table convention that Kaedim's YAM harness and SIMPACT already ship; (2) the specific finding that LLM-named-material + measured table beats LLM direct numbers on real motion (route exists in NeRF2Physics, but has never been scored on motion); (3) a small measured mu_pair / rho_eff-by-build table with IQR for ~11-25 materials -- call it a table, not an atlas. Reposition against Physics 101 as 'same footage, upgraded protocol: per-material transfer instead of a learned CNN, metric trajectory error instead of correlation, physical re-simulation instead of a frame regressor', and correct the characterisations of PhysVid (it does hold out objects and surfaces) and EKFPhys (measured-vs-estimate, not closed loop). Demote the mass-within-25% row: held-out mass-from-photo is already standard on ABO-500; the only increment is measured mass+volume and build-aware density. Cite Kaedim 2610.00731 (r 0.51 -> 0.90, confounded with scale and visuals) as partial evidence on the 'does it matter' question instead of calling it fully open.
verdicts.summary: The broad claim is refuted on the proposal's own data: Physics 101 (BMVC 2016) already runs a split-by-object protocol with outcome prediction on unseen objects, and Galileo (NeurIPS 2015) already does the 10-deg-from-20-deg stays/slides transfer over 50 objects -- the same footage, the same held-out-object idea, a weaker scorer. Two of the seven named prior works are mischaracterised (PhysVid does hold out objects and surfaces; EKFPhys is estimate-vs-measured, not closed-loop). The 'material class -> per-class table' assignment layer is already deployed and policy-level-validated against real robot trials by Kaedim's YAM harness (arXiv 2610.00731, released this week), and held-out mass-from-photo is standard on ABO-500. What genuinely remains open, from primary sources checked: no work scores ASSIGNMENT routes (released sim-ready generators, LLM numbers, per-class tables) by re-simulating assigned parameters against per-object real trajectories with a repeat-trial floor, and no measured per-material friction/density table with uncertainty for household rigid materials exists in simulator-ready form. GAUGE, PhysX-Bench and UniPhys-Bench are characterised fairly. Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out after ~20 queries, so 2026 preprint coverage is incomplete; treat 'not found' as medium confidence. Score 4.5/10: the narrowed protocol-plus-table contribution survives, the headline novelty and two prior-work characterisations do not.

evidence: Every external dependency exists today (verified 2026-10-07): PhysX-Anything code github.com/ziangcao0312/PhysX-Anything + weights huggingface.co/Caoza/PhysX-Anything (base Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, weights MIT, code S-Lab; outputs per-part density + absolute scale + URDF, NOT friction); UniPhysGen code released 2026-08-30 at github.com/breezexian/UniPhysGen with four HF checkpoints incl. breezexian/UniPhysGen-1.7B-Physics (Qwen3-1.7B + Sonata, F32 ~2B params, weights CC BY-NC 4.0, code Apache-2.0; input = part-segmented point cloud .npz, image optional; outputs material, density, friction, object scale/mass); UniPhys-40K and UniPhys-Bench released; PhysXNet annotations on HF datasets/Caoza/PhysX-3D (per-part material/density strings, GPL-3.0 + ShapeNet terms, ungated) -- so the coverage number is computable.

Local resources suffice: GPUs 1-5 of the 8 A6000s idle at 2 MiB each; CUDA 12.8/12.9 toolchain present; the LLM gateway key is present; Physics 101 is on disk (data/phys101, 6.1 GB, 103 object photos, ramp + fall scenarios); the e1 scorer (scripts/e1_heldout.py, 293 lines) re-runs in seconds in the warp env. Home disk is 98% full (96 GB free) -- two new conda envs plus 7B+2B weights fit but go on the NAS (15 TB free).

Two heavy new environments stand between now and the first experiment: PhysX-Anything pins transformers==4.50.0 (cosmos env is 5.14.1) and needs xformers/flash-attn/diffoctreerast/spconv/mipgaussian/kaolin/nvdiffrast built from source; UniPhysGen needs Sonata/Pointcept + its own torch stack and a part-segmentation step before inference (the PhysX-Anything -> UniPhysGen hand-off is a mesh->segmented-point-cloud conversion nobody has run). For one researcher this is 1-2 weeks of install churn on its own; the 'two weeks' first-experiment estimate is optimistic by about 2x.

MEASURED TODAY on the stored e1 data: the benchmark's response to the assigned mu is exactly flat above the 20-degree threshold. Median held-out RMS vs assigned mu: 0.05->48.1, 0.10->28.1, 0.15->10.0, 0.20->4.7, 0.25->4.9, 0.30->24.4, 0.35->72.0, 0.40/0.45/0.50/0.55/0.60 -> 87.8 mm identically (np.allclose True for mu 0.37 vs 0.60). Any route that emits a generic >= 0.36 (LLMs measured at ~0.4 in f14; generators plausibly the same) scores one identical number, so the first experiment cannot RANK generator routes against each other or against 'generic 0.40' -- only the one-bit stays/slides survives. The plan's own 'biggest risk' is the default outcome, and its fix (30-40 degree phone ramp) is scheduled for weeks 5-8, after the headline experiment.

MEASURED TODAY: kill test (2) as pre-registered FAILS on the existing data. 'RMS at (material median +/- 0.05) must exceed the oracle p90 (6.2 mm) for >= 40 of 70 objects': both-sides reading 28/70 (material median) or 39/70 (object's own median mu); either-side reading 63/70 or 48/70. At +/- 0.02 -- the size of the table-vs-oracle gap (median |dmu| 0.017 vs 0.010) and of the within-material IQR the atlas proposes to ship as a measured DR range -- only 4/70 objects resolve it. The benchmark can separate routes that differ by >= 0.05 pooled (LLM number 7.5 mm vs table 2.6 mm, p = 1e-7 already), but cannot validate the atlas's per-material uncertainty per object.

Ramp segments are short: median 0.63 s (~19 frames at 29.97/30 fps), min 0.20 s, max 2.1 s over 360 trials; 70 sliding objects over 11 materials; 20-degree 'stays' are dominated by h_rubber 36, foam 35, rubber 23, m_coin 20 clips -- the three never-sliding materials have no friction row until the phone ramp exists, and that ramp is a different surface requiring a second anchor (the atlas becomes two-surface).

Physics 101 licence: the shipped readme (phys101/readme.txt, v1.0 Jan 2017) and phys101.csail.mit.edu state no licence or redistribution terms; a web claim of 'MIT License' came from an unrelated HF mirror. Releasing our tracks/splits as derived data is defensible with attribution; redistributing clips is not, so the benchmark must be 'download Physics 101 + our tracks/splits' and the authors should be asked.

Differentiable physics and 'beyond rooms' are not dependencies of this plan at all: the scorer is a closed-form parabola (traj_rms in e1_heldout.py) and Newton is forward-only (p4). Not a feasibility blocker, but the plan does not deliver the user's stated requirement (a) and reframes (c) as catalogue coverage.

No robot, no mocap, no 240 fps capture is needed: sliding at 30-60 fps with scale from a known board length / object edge (p1's camera-scale invariant, 1633-1724 px/m) is the only capture required; restitution is out of scope. Phone-ramp metric scale and side-view geometry replicate the Physics 101 setup and are feasible with a tripod in 2-3 days.
verdicts.surviving_form: Keep the benchmark + atlas plan but re-sequence and re-register it: (1) swap weeks 1-2 and 5-8 -- capture the 30/40-degree phone ramp FIRST (it is the only way the benchmark can rank routes that emit mu >= 0.36, which is where LLMs and probably both generators sit; without it the first experiment returns one identical 87.8 mm for every generic route and ranks nothing); state the second surface anchor up front and report the atlas as mu_pair per surface. (2) Budget 3-4 weeks, not 2, for the first experiment: two fresh CUDA-extension environments (transformers 4.50 for the 7B PhysX-Anything, Sonata/Pointcept for UniPhysGen) plus the untested mesh -> segmented point-cloud hand-off; run the PhysX-Anything density-x-measured-volume mass test alone in week 1 since it needs only the VLM stage. (3) Re-write kill test 2 to what the data can pass: specify 'either side' or use the object's own mu as the centre, and drop the claim that the atlas IQR (0.01-0.05) is validated per object -- only 4/70 objects resolve +/- 0.02; report the atlas uncertainty as measured repeat spread, validated pooled. (4) Note PhysX-Anything emits density and scale but not friction, so the single-photo friction route is PhysX-Anything -> UniPhysGen only, with the friction convention anchor audited as a scale. (5) Release tracks/splits/scorer, not Physics 101 frames, and write to the dataset authors about derived-data redistribution. (6) Say plainly that the differentiable engine is not used and that scale is addressed as catalogue coverage, or pair this with a second proposal that does use the tape.
verdicts.summary: Not refuted: everything the 90-day plan depends on exists and is obtainable -- PhysX-Anything (code + 7B weights), UniPhysGen (code and four 1.7B checkpoints released 2026-08-30, CC BY-NC), PhysXNet material annotations, Physics 101 on disk, five idle A6000s, the gateway, and a scorer that runs today. But the two-week first experiment is optimistic by about 2x (two heavy CUDA-extension environments and an untested mesh-to-segmented-point-cloud hand-off), and two measurements made today on the stored e1 data cut into what that experiment can say: the 20-degree benchmark's response is exactly flat above mu = 0.364 (identical 87.8 mm RMS for 0.37-0.60), so every generic route scores one number and cannot be ranked until the 30-40 degree phone ramp exists (scheduled after the headline); and the pre-registered rule-1 kill test fails as written (28-39 of 70 objects resolve +/- 0.05 on both sides against the required 40; 4 of 70 resolve +/- 0.02, the scale of the atlas IQR the plan wants to ship as measured uncertainty). Physics 101 carries no stated licence, so clips cannot be redistributed, only tracks and splits. The plan survives re-sequenced (phone ramp first, 3-4 weeks for the generator chain, kill test rewritten) and with the honest note that it uses no differentiable physics and reframes scale as catalogue coverage.

evidence: Effect size is small in absolute terms: docs/results/e1_heldout.json gives material 2.55 mm median / 12.4 p90, dataset-wide single constant 4.4 / 15.4 mm, LLM number 7.5 / 44.9 mm, oracle 1.77 / 6.2 mm. On a 20 deg ramp at mu~0.23 the slide is ~10-20 cm over the tracked window, so every route except the LLM number is within 2-4% of the trajectory; knowing the material buys 1.8 mm median over assigning one constant to everything. dmu medians are 0.010 (oracle) / 0.017 (material) / 0.019 (pipeline) / 0.052 (LLM). A catalogue builder does not change practice over delta-mu = 0.03.

The benchmark is one observable of a one-parameter law (s = s0 + 0.5 a t^2 with a = g(sin a - mu cos a)) on one board at one informative angle; its own identifiability window is mu in [0.1, 0.36] and 3 of 15 materials (foam, rubber, hollow rubber) plus coins never slide. The materials that matter most for manipulation and locomotion (rubber, fabric, glass, painted metal) are either unmeasured or the 'phone ramp extension' that is weeks 5-8 of the plan, on a different surface with its own anchor.

The proposal explicitly declines two of the user's three axes: 'Gradients buy little here... This paper would be the same paper on a non-differentiable engine' and "'Beyond rooms' is the wrong axis". The relayed user request (differentiable physics; practical system for robots or simulations; interactable worlds at scale) wins over the computed task, and this proposal answers only 'practical for simulations' and only as a lookup table.

No downstream consequence can be shown: the proposal's own 'Honest limit' cites SIMPLER (<=15% sensitivity to object physics) and the Push-T MPC finding ('mass and friction yield no stable adaptation signal'); with no robot the paper cannot demonstrate that the atlas changes any policy, grasp or sim-to-real outcome. The consumer story ('BEHAVIOR-1K / SimReady / UrbanVerse replace VLM numbers with the atlas JSON') is asserted, not evidenced; those catalogues' objects are furniture-scale and multi-surface, while the atlas is mu_pair against one whiteboard for 7 cm cubes, poles and toys, transferred through a geometric-mean rule with an assumed anchor (body mu = mu_pair^2 / 0.45) checked on 8 materials at 0.75-1.05.

Scoring released generators (PhysX-Anything, UniPhysGen) on 7 cm Physics 101 objects is, by the proposal's own 'biggest risk', off their training distribution and may not rank them at all: if they emit a generic ~0.4 (as f14 measured for LLMs: 0.31-0.47 for everything) every route reads 'stays' at 20 deg and the benchmark reports a uniform failure. The likely headline is 'generators are no better than a dataset-wide median', which is one bit and already predictable from f14 and e1.

The core numbers already exist in scripts/e1_heldout.py; the 90-day plan's new work is two generator inferences (hours), LLM gateway calls, string-matching catalogue vocabularies to table rows, and a phone-ramp capture. Rows added at week 10 (13 project assets re-parameterised, outcome shift VLM vs atlas) are a demo, not a measurement anyone else needs. Venue fit is a NeurIPS D&B / workshop benchmark paper on 2016 footage (Galileo and Physics 101 already fit physics to these clips), not a top-venue systems or robotics contribution.

Kill test (1) is well designed but its pass condition is close to what f14/e1 already measured, so the pre-registered outcome is low-information; kill test (2) ('RMS at material median +/- 0.05 must exceed oracle p90 for >= 40 of 70 objects') is a real rule-1 audit of the benchmark and is the one genuinely new result in the plan.
verdicts.surviving_form: Keep the e1 protocol and the rule-1 audit of the benchmark (kill test 2) as a short benchmark/dataset release — the first real-held-out-motion score of released sim-ready generators is publishable at a D&B or workshop venue, and the two-week first experiment should be run exactly as written because it is cheap and settles the 'reinventing the wheel' worry either way. Drop the atlas-as-product and catalogue-coverage framing unless kill test 1 passes AND the phone-ramp extension lifts rubber/foam/fabric/glass, since without those rows no catalogue builder gains anything over a dataset-wide constant. To meet the user's actual ask, the benchmark must become multi-observable: 240 fps phone capture of real objects under drop, topple and push/shove (3-6 parameters per clip, where the validated differentiable contact kernels do the inversion and the per-clip error bars are Jacobian-based), with the consumer defined as a 'photo -> material name (LLM, 80%) -> measured (mu, rho, e, CoM-by-build) with uncertainty' assignment library whose outputs are scored on real motion it never fitted. That is a system, not a table, and it is the only version that is both actionable and uses the differentiable engine for something the forward model cannot do. 'Interactable worlds at scale' should be stated as out of scope rather than redefined as catalogue coverage.
verdicts.summary: Under the impact lens the proposal is refuted as written: its headline is a 1.8-5 mm difference in a 10-20 cm slide on one board, equivalent to delta-mu ~0.03, with no demonstrable downstream consequence (the proposal itself cites SIMPLER and Push-T showing insensitivity and admits no robot); the measured atlas covers only materials that slide at 20 deg on a whiteboard and omits the ones manipulation cares about; the generator-scoring hook is likely to return one bit ('generic 0.4, stays') that f14/e1 already predict; and it explicitly declines the user's differentiable-physics and scale axes. It is an honest, cheap, publishable benchmark note (D&B / workshop), not a top-venue system, and the only part worth running immediately is the two-week generator-scoring experiment plus the rule-1 audit of the benchmark. It survives only narrowed to that, or extended into a multi-observable real-motion benchmark where the differentiable engine does per-clip inversion and the output is an assignment library with uncertainty.

proposals.title: IMPACT ATLAS: restitution and contact-law calibration for everyday materials from 240 fps phone drops, with the differentiable exact-mesh plane contact as the per-clip inversion instrument
proposals.thesis: Restitution is the parameter no asset pipeline carries and no multi-material dataset measures (Bounce-and-Learn: one ball on many surfaces; GAUGE: three rigid materials; PhysVid: hand-annotated apex heights; our p3 at 30 fps failed on frame rate, not method). A 240 fps phone with two independent routes (video apex heights and audio inter-impact intervals), ten repeats per object, and a Hunt-Crossley alpha fitted through our validated body-plane contact yields e(v) with uncertainty for ~15 materials and answers a question GAUGE left open: when Newton's bouncing ball is 15-22x off the real floor, is the parameter wrong or the law?
proposals.what_we_build: (1) A capture protocol: phone at 240 fps on a tripod, two LED lights for short exposure, audio recorded; two surfaces (a wooden board standing in for the Physics 101 ramp board and the project's table, and a steel/glass plate); two drop heights 0.15 / 0.45 m (impact 1.7 / 3.0 m/s); 10 repeats; 30-60 objects covering the Physics 101 classes (cardboard, wood, plastic, porcelain, rubber, foam, metal) and the asset classes with no row (books/paper, leather baseball, apple, glazed ceramic, PLA/ABS prints), each with mass (kitchen scale) and volume (dimensions or displacement). (2) Readout: p3's CoTracker3 multi-track pipeline at 240 fps; e_h = sqrt(h_bounce / h_drop), e_t from the inter-impact interval ratio read from video AND from the audio clicks (pixel-independent), and g from the free-fall parabola as the scale invariant (fixed camera => constant). Spheres first, then blocks and shapes. (3) Engine side: alpha per material from the sphere data at two speeds (e ~ 1 - alpha v, the law our rigs already use), then for non-spherical objects a per-clip gradient fit of (alpha, mu, landing orientation; shell vs solid CoM chosen by build) through the tape-safe DiffMeshScene over the first impact only, with a Jacobian-based (Fisher) error bar, batched over hundreds of clips; CEM fallback where tape != FD. (4) Deliverables: atlas rows (e at two speeds, alpha, IQR, n, surface) joined to the Physics 101 (mu, rho) rows; a per-material alpha table for src/sim/rigs.py replacing the assumed alpha = 0.4; an engine-fidelity report (simulated apex height and time-to-second-impact vs measured, normalised by repeat spread) comparable to GAUGE's bouncing-ball row; the 13 assets' bounce/settle probes re-run with measured alpha.
proposals.builds_on_our_assets: scripts/p3_restitution.py (two-route design, CoTracker3 dense tracks with forward/backward queries, table-line logic -- failed only because 30 fps gave ~5 blurred frames and a 2.7x g spread); docs/results/p7_cd_restitution.json (e vs cd/mass curves on both rigs) and scripts/p8_alpha.py + src/sim/rigs.py + MeshProbeScene.set_restitution_alpha (restitution as alpha, measured identical for 0.1 and 0.4 kg, both rigs within 0.04-0.07); p5_transfer.cd_for_restitution; scripts/g0_grad_check.py's tape-safe DiffMeshScene (per-step buffers; tape = FD for d(slide)/dmu through the exact-mesh PLANE contact); src/sim/diff_drop.py and the M13/M14 pipeline (restitution damping recovered from a rendered single bounce at 15-28% error, with the finding that the horizon must end after the first rebound); build-aware CoM/inertia (shell/solid, textbook-exact to 1%); the bounce probe (rho = -0.995) and its sensitivity row (cd 5.73x, mu-immune); p101_density.json for the mass of matching classes; the 13 assets.
proposals.differentiable_physics_role: Split honestly. For spheres: zero -- e comes from two closed-form routes and alpha from e at two speeds; no gradient is needed and none should be used. For non-spherical objects (cubes landing on an edge, the teapot, the toy shark): the rebound depends jointly on alpha, mu, the landing orientation and the CoM model, a 4-6-D per-clip inversion where a grid is impractical; the body-plane adjoint is validated (g0: tape matches central FD; M13/M14 recovered damping through one bounce), and the horizon stops after the first rebound because the project measured that gradients through continuous/settling contact explode. So gradients buy: per-clip multi-parameter identification, a Fisher error bar from the Jacobian at the optimum, and batching hundreds of clips per GPU. What they do not buy: the body-body pair adjoint is still broken (g0c: tape -0.03 vs FD -0.38) -- irrelevant for drops onto a plane, but this proposal does not fix it; and if the per-clip landscape is rugged, CEM is the fallback, as the project has already had to do twice.
proposals.scale_claim: Not rooms: materials x impact speeds x impact classes, with uncertainty. Concretely 30-60 objects / ~15 materials / 2 surfaces / 2 speeds / 10 repeats = 1,200-2,400 clips in 3-4 capture days; joined with the Physics 101 rows this gives an atlas of ~20 materials x (mu, rho, e, alpha) with IQRs -- the first table of that shape anywhere. The scale metric is the same catalogue coverage as Proposal 1 (share of PhysXNet / UniPhys-40K material strings with a measured e row), and 'beyond rooms' enters only through what consumes the table: a 100k-asset catalogue gets a restitution column at zero marginal cost. Mocap-grade precision per clip is NOT claimed; breadth plus repeat-based uncertainty is.
proposals.practicality: Users: (1) Newton/Warp users and the project itself get a measured alpha per material in place of the assumed 0.4 (every tilt-rig probe currently runs on it); (2) catalogue builders get the first restitution column with uncertainty for SimReady physics:restitution / MJCF, with an explicit mapping from Hunt-Crossley alpha to PhysX's scalar e at a stated impact speed (the two are not the same quantity -- that mapping is part of the deliverable); (3) engine developers get a calibration dataset that separates parameter error from law error on everyday materials, extending GAUGE's bouncing-ball row from 3 materials to ~15; (4) authored assets with no Physics 101 class (books, baseball, apple) finally get measured rows for mass and e. Limits: a phone is not a NOKOV rig; non-spherical impact results may have to be reported per impact class rather than as one alpha; policy-transfer value is untested, as in Proposal 1. On its own this is a dataset + calibration paper; with Proposal 1 it completes the assignment layer.
proposals.novelty_argument: Three scouts list the same holes: no multi-material restitution dataset at an adequate frame rate; no calibration of a penalty / Hunt-Crossley law against measured e across masses and speeds; and GAUGE's finding that engines are worst on impulsive contact with no diagnosis of whether law or parameter is at fault. Differences: vs Bounce-and-Learn, object materials rather than surfaces and measured e rather than a learned effective one; vs GAUGE, ~15 materials instead of 3, a law calibration instead of a score, and a phone instead of 16 mocap cameras (less precise, far cheaper, repeatable by anyone); vs the ContactNets / Dojo / DiffMJX cube toss, 30-60 objects with worse per-clip pose precision than 148 Hz AprilTags, traded for breadth and material-level uncertainty; vs PhysVid's elasticity split, two automatic routes and a closed loop through a simulator. Small-difference honesty: for a sphere this is a textbook lab exercise; the contribution is breadth, the two-route protocol, measured uncertainty, and the engine calibration -- and the gradient part is only load-bearing for non-spherical impacts, which may turn out too chaotic to carry a stable alpha (DiffMJX reports trajectory error stuck above 0.25 from corner impacts).
nearest_prior_work: Bounce and Learn (arXiv 1904.06827, ICLR 2019): 5K RGB-D bounces of ONE foam ball on many surfaces; restitution learned as an effective latent, never measured

GAUGE (arXiv 2608.05948): restitution on an air-bearing rail for wood/plastic/metal, 180 Hz mocap; Newton bouncing ball normalised RMSE 22.71 with stock solvers -- the number this proposal tries to explain
PhysVid (arXiv 2510.02311): 100 real bounce clips with manually annotated apex heights; estimators only, no re-simulation

ContactNets cube toss (arXiv 2009.11193), Dojo (2203.00806), DiffMJX (2506.14186): one acrylic cube, 148 Hz AprilTags, contact parameters fitted per object; the de-facto real contact benchmark, with higher precision and one object

IRIS (arXiv 2603.16432, HF rasulkhanbayov/IRIS): 240 real 4K/60 fps videos with instrument-measured parameters and 10 repeats (sliding cone, dropping ball, pendulums) -- used here as an external check of the tracking-to-fit pipeline against instrument GT, not as a bounce source
Our p3 (failed at 30 fps: g spread 2.7x, route correlation 0.38), p7/p8 (alpha formulation), M13/M14 (damping recovered from rendered single bounces at 15-28%)
first_90_days: Weeks 1-2 (first experiment): 10 objects (5 balls/near-spheres, 5 Physics-101-class blocks) x 10 drops from 0.3 m onto the wooden board at 240 fps with audio; p3 tracker at 240 fps; per clip e_h, e_t(video), e_t(audio), g from the parabola. Decide the instrument gate.

Weeks 2-3: rule-1 on the engine: simulate each sphere at measured size and mass with alpha swept on the bounce rig and the tilt rig; show the apex and the inter-impact time move with alpha (range vs repeat spread) and follow e ~ 1 - alpha v; fit one alpha per material at both heights; residual vs repeat IQR. Run the p3 pipeline on IRIS's dropping-ball / sliding-cone videos as an external check against instrument GT with uncertainty.

Weeks 3-6: full capture: 30-60 objects, 2 surfaces, 2 heights, 10 repeats; masses and volumes; include books, baseball, apple, glazed ceramic, cardboard box, plastic toy, metal pot stand-ins so every project asset class gets a row; seeded, cached tracking.

Weeks 6-9: non-spherical objects: per-clip gradient fit of (alpha, mu, landing orientation) through DiffMeshScene over the first impact; tape-vs-FD check on 5 clips before any fit is trusted; repeat-CV and orientation-invariance tests; CEM where the tape fails.

Weeks 9-11: engine-fidelity report: simulated apex height and time-to-second-impact vs measured over all clips, normalised by repeat spread, by material and speed; identify where a scalar alpha fails (speed dependence, plastic/visco materials) and report e(v) there instead.

Weeks 11-13: atlas v1 (mu, rho, e, alpha with IQR/n) and the per-material alpha table in rigs.py; re-run the bounce/settle probes on the 13 assets with measured alpha; package clips, tracks, scorer; write-up with the pre-registered gates reported as they fell.
proposals.first_experiment: 100 drops (10 objects x 10 repeats, 0.3 m, wooden board, 240 fps + audio): median two-route disagreement |e_video - e_audio| (target < 0.03), repeat CV of e per object (target < 10%), and the spread of g recovered from the free-fall parabolas across clips (target < 3%; p3 at 30 fps gave 2.7x). One week of capture and tracking on one A6000; the number decides whether the phone is an instrument.
proposals.kill_test: Decided now, before any full capture. (1) Instrument gate: on spheres, if the median |e_h - e_t| exceeds 0.05 or the parabola-g spread across clips exceeds 5%, the phone pipeline is dead (p3's failure mode, now at 240 fps) and no further capture happens. (2) Rule 1 on the engine: the simulated apex must move with alpha by more than 3x the repeat spread over the alpha range implied by the real materials, and one alpha per material must reproduce e at BOTH drop speeds within the repeat IQR for >= 10 of ~15 materials; otherwise the result is the negative finding 'a scalar Hunt-Crossley alpha cannot carry real restitution across speeds', the atlas ships e(v) only, and the engine-calibration claim is withdrawn. (3) Non-spheres: the gradient-fitted alpha must be repeat-stable (CV < 15% over 10 drops) and independent of landing orientation (orientation fitted per clip); if not, the gradient story shrinks to spheres and the atlas reports e per impact class.
proposals.resources: A 240 fps-capable phone (iPhone slo-mo 1080p240 or Android equivalent), tripod, two LED lights (exposure ~1/2000 s), a wooden board and a steel/glass plate, kitchen scale (0.1 g), calipers, ~40-60 household objects; 3-4 capture days. One A6000 for CoTracker3 at 240 fps (~250 frames per drop, 1,200-2,400 clips) and the batched tape fits; the second GPU only during the fit sweeps. No robot, no mocap.
proposals.biggest_risk: Phone optics: at 3 m/s an object moves 12 mm per frame, motion blur depends on exposure (needs bright light), and rolling-shutter skew distorts fast vertical motion -- the two-route design is built to expose this, and the audio route does not depend on pixels at all, so the capture can fail honestly rather than silently. Second: non-spherical impacts are chaotic (corner strikes), so a per-clip alpha may not be repeat-stable and the differentiable-inversion part may reduce to spheres, leaving a dataset paper without the engine-identification story. Third: without mocap-grade pose, our per-clip precision is below ContactNets'; reviewers may prefer one precise cube to sixty imprecise objects, so the uncertainty must be reported per row and the GAUGE/IRIS cross-checks must be in the paper.
proposals.expected_headline_result: Expected if everything works: a 240 fps phone protocol with two independent routes (video apex heights, audio inter-impact timing) measures the restitution of ~50 everyday objects across ~15 materials to +/-0.02 with repeat-based uncertainty -- the first multi-material restitution table -- and a single Hunt-Crossley alpha per material, fitted through differentiable exact-mesh contact, reproduces the measured rebounds across a 2x impact-speed range within the repeat spread for most materials, locating the engine's remaining impulsive-contact error in the law rather than the parameter.

evidence: Sphere restitution vs impact speed per material from high-speed drop video is a mature measurement literature, not an open hole: Kuwabara & Kono 1987 (JJAP 26:1230, viscoelastic e(v) across materials); Labous et al. 1997 (NJIT, 'Measurements of collisional properties of spheres using high-speed video analysis'); Cross, AJP 67:222 (1999) 'The bounce of a ball' (many ball types); Muller, Heckel, Sack, Poschel PRL 2013 (cris.fau.de/publications/109831744) automated large-n e(v) measurement showing OSCILLATIONS superimposed on the known decay -- a direct threat to the proposal's scalar e ~ 1 - alpha*v per material. The e ~ 1 - alpha v form is Hunt & Crossley 1975 itself.

Calibrating a damping/restitution law against drop tests across materials and speeds is routine in DEM: Yurata et al., Adv. Powder Technol. 32(4):1004 (2021) (mfix.netl.doe.gov/citation-post/2021-yurata-tarabordin-journal/) -- glass and polypropylene beads on acrylic and steel plates, high-speed camera drop test, COR fitted as a function of material, impact velocity and temperature and used in DEM; Itasca PFC docs calibrate the normal critical damping ratio to restitution (docs.itascacg.com/pfc700/.../cmlinear_restitution.html). Haptics HC parameter identification across materials (Queen's thesis 'Identification and Rendering of Contact Dynamic Models', queensu.scholaris.ca) is also established.

The audio route is old and its validity limit is already measured: Bernstein 1977 AJP 'Listening to the coefficient of restitution' (also arXiv physics/0210092 'Listening to the COR and g of a bouncing ball'); Phyphox acoustic-stopwatch COR labs with video cross-checks are standard physics-education practice (e-journal.usd.ac.id IJASST 4548; jurnal.untirta.ac.id JPPI 13400; 'Measuring COR for tennis and golf balls using smartphone sensors', ir.swu.ac.th). Crucially Heckel, Glielmo, Gunkelmann, Poschel, Phys. Rev. E 93, 032901 (2016): 'the well-established method to measure the coefficient of restitution through the emitted sound is applicable only for the case of nearly perfect spheres'; shape deviations dominate the error, and air drag matters at larger heights. The proposal's audio e_t for blocks, teapots and sharks is invalidated by this before capture.

Law-vs-parameter diagnosis on real impacts already done for robotics engines: Acosta, Yang, Posa, 'Validating Robotics Simulators on Real-World Impacts', arXiv 2110.00541 (RA-L/IROS 2022): 550 real tosses of a 10 cm acrylic cube on a wooden table at 148 Hz mocap; stiffness, damping and friction identified per simulator (Drake, MuJoCo, Bullet) by minimising trajectory error, with stiffness/damping sweeps at fixed friction; conclusion that the simulators 'produced less restitution than observed in the real system' and none reproduced the observed elasticity -- i.e. law error, not parameter error. The proposal does not cite this, although it is the closest prior to its 'engine-fidelity report'.

GAUGE, arXiv 2608.05948 (Aug 2026): restitution measured on an air-bearing rail (e = v_out/v_in) for wood, plastic, metal AND rubber (four, not three), 16 NOKOV cameras at 180 Hz, 20 trials per task, uncertainty annotations, dataset on Hugging Face (huggingface.co/datasets/introvoyz042/GAUGE-Dataset, mirror -- medium confidence on official status); bouncing-ball task is rubber only; Newton RMSE 22.71 vs baseline 5.29, Isaac 15.63, Genesis 22.50; engine parameters set from measured metadata, not fitted. The proposal's characterisation is broadly fair but understates material count and omits the 20-trial repeats.

Gradient-based restitution/friction identification from REAL video already exists: DiffSDFSim, arXiv 2111.15318 (tennis-ball bounce from a RealSense D455, optimising restitution and friction); PIN-WM, arXiv 2504.16693 (friction and restitution via differentiable physics from visual observations, real-world sim2real); ContactNets 2009.11193 / Dojo 2203.00806 / DiffMJX 2506.14186 cube-toss fits. The 'per-clip multi-parameter inversion with Fisher error bars' is an incremental extension, not a new capability.

Phone-captured real benchmarks with instrument GT now exist and mostly skip restitution, which is the one part of the hole that survives: WorldBench arXiv 2601.21282 (iPhone 13 slow-motion, 234 real videos: gravity 51, viscosity 80, friction 103 on wood/rubber/sandpaper/plastic; no restitution); IRIS arXiv 2603.16432 (4K/60 fps, 10 trials per setting, dropping/falling ball, pendulum, sliding cone; no restitution -- proposal's characterisation correct); PhysVid arXiv 2510.02311 (real elasticity split from YouTube + iPhone slow-mo, basketball/tennis/balloon/.../tomato, e 0.44-0.98, manual height annotation, no re-simulation -- proposal's '100 clips' count not verified by me, medium confidence); PISA Experiments arXiv 2503.09595 (361 real household-object drop videos, apparently without restitution GT -- low confidence, abstract only).
Bounce and Learn arXiv 1904.06827: 5K RGB-D bounces, one foam ball, restitution learned as a latent -- proposal's characterisation is accurate.

Sim-ready asset pipelines (PhysX-Anything arXiv 2511.13648, PhysXNet arXiv 2507.12465) annotate material/density via VLM with no measured restitution; NVIDIA SimReady foundation requires physics:restitution as a USD attribute with no provenance requirement visible on the requirements page (nvidia.github.io/simready-foundation). A measured, uncertainty-bearing restitution column validated against held-out real motion is still absent from catalogues -- this is the surviving gap.
verdicts.surviving_form: Drop the claims that are textbook or already published: (a) sphere e(v) by high-speed drop video and its e ~ 1 - alpha v fit (Kuwabara-Kono, Cross, Labous, Hunt-Crossley 1975, DEM calibration such as Yurata 2021); (b) the audio inter-impact route as a general second route -- per Heckel et al. PRE 2016 it is valid only for near-perfect spheres, so use it as the instrument gate on spheres ONLY and never as e_t for blocks or assets; (c) 'differentiable identification of restitution from real video' as a capability (DiffSDFSim, PIN-WM, ContactNets); (d) 'engines fail on elastic impact because of the law, not the parameter' as a finding (Acosta et al. 2022 already showed it on 550 cube tosses across Drake/MuJoCo/Bullet; cite it). What remains open and defensible: (1) a public material-level table of (mu, rho, e(v), alpha) with repeat IQRs for ~15-20 EVERYDAY materials matched to asset classes and joined to the Physics 101 rows -- a dataset/resource contribution, framed as such, with WorldBench/IRIS/GAUGE named as the benchmarks that omit restitution; (2) the specific Newton/Warp question GAUGE and Acosta leave open: does ONE Hunt-Crossley alpha per material, fitted at one speed on one surface, predict the second speed AND the second surface (restitution is a pair property, so cross-surface transfer of a per-material alpha is the genuinely untested claim, and Muller et al. 2013's non-monotone e(v) is the pre-registered failure mode); (3) non-spherical, orientation-dependent first-impact inversion from a phone at catalogue breadth, with repeat-stability as the gate, anchored against the public ContactNets acrylic-cube data as a precision reference; (4) the differentiator from PhysX/SimReady pipelines: the assigned restitution is validated on the real motion of HELD-OUT objects, as the project already did for friction (e1). Pitch it as a calibration-dataset paper with an engine-transfer test, not as a new measurement method.
verdicts.summary: The core idea -- measure restitution of many materials from high-speed drop video, read it two ways (apex heights and inter-impact timing, including from sound), fit a velocity-dependent Hunt-Crossley damping per material, and ask whether a physics engine's bouncing error is law or parameter -- exists in pieces across the sphere-impact physics literature (Kuwabara-Kono 1987, Cross 1999, Labous 1997, Muller et al. PRL 2013), DEM/haptics contact calibration (Yurata 2021, Itasca), the audio-route physics-education literature (Bernstein 1977, Phyphox labs) and robotics (Acosta-Yang-Posa 2022 on 550 real cube tosses, which already concluded Drake/MuJoCo/Bullet under-produce restitution by construction; DiffSDFSim and PIN-WM for gradient-based restitution ID from real video). Two uncited primary results cut against the design: Heckel et al. PRE 2016 shows the sound-timing route is valid only for near-perfect spheres (so the audio e_t for blocks and assets is dead on arrival), and Muller et al. 2013 shows e(v) is non-monotone with oscillations (so a scalar alpha per material is a pre-registered risk, not a discovery). The nearest-work list is mostly fair (Bounce and Learn, IRIS, PhysVid accurate; GAUGE has four materials and 20 trials, not three) but omits Acosta et al. 2022, the closest prior to the engine-fidelity claim. What survives is narrower than the title: no public phone-era benchmark (WorldBench, IRIS, PhysVid, GAUGE) provides a multi-material restitution table with repeat uncertainty for everyday materials joined to friction and density, no sim-ready catalogue carries a measured restitution column validated on held-out real motion, and the cross-speed AND cross-surface transfer of a per-material Hunt-Crossley alpha in Newton is untested. That is a dataset-plus-calibration contribution, not a new measurement method, and should be pitched as such.

verdicts.lens: FEASIBILITY (first experiment in 2 weeks; 90-day milestone; hidden dependencies: metric scale/camera geometry, contact gradients in Newton 1.4, frame rate, licences, GPU budget, one researcher, no rig)
evidence: Contact gradient through an IMPACT on the validated exact-mesh plane contact was NOT previously demonstrated (g0 covered sliding only; M13/M14 covered impact on the retired sphere-cover solver, PROJECT_LOG.md lines 721-775). I ran it now (scratch script impact_grad.py, solid 7 cm cube dropped 0.20 m, tilt-rig pen_frac 1e-4, loss = body height 0.22 s after impact, tape vs central FD on cd): at 420 substeps, flat landing, ratio tape/FD = 0.999 / 1.000 / 1.098 at cd = 0.5x / 1x / 2x the alpha=0.4 value; 20-degree edge landing 1.001 / 1.170 / 0.973; cost 1.5 s and 0.41 GB per forward+backward, 4200 steps, 386 vertices. At 100 substeps and the deadest cd the sign flips (ratio -14.6). So the per-clip gradient fit is real for the first impact at the tilt rig's step rate, degrades to ~10-17% error on edge landings and dead materials, and must not be run at coarse substeps.
scripts/g0_grad_check.py re-run on GPU 1: d(slide)/d(mu) tape -0.5448 vs FD -0.5453, 0.4 s per 1200-step tape -- the tape-safe DiffMeshScene exists and works as claimed.

Hunt-Crossley alpha is already a scalar transform of the differentiable cd array (src/sim/mesh_scene.py:312-342, cd = 1.5*alpha*k/HC; HC term inside ground_contact_mesh at src/sim/mesh_contact.py:101), so fitting alpha needs no new kernel.

scripts/p3_restitution.py exists with the two-route (velocity + height) design, CoTracker3 dense forward/backward tracking and table-line logic; docs/results/p3_restitution_summary.json shows the 30 fps failure (e_h 0.05-0.34 with physics inverted). Only the frame rate and the trim/segmentation change for 240 fps clips (250 frames per drop, within cotracker3_offline's capacity).

IRIS dataset verified on HuggingFace (rasulkhanbayov/IRIS): 240 videos, 3840x2160 at 60 fps, 8 classes x 3 settings x 10 takes, instrument-measured parameters in parameters.json, CC-BY-NC-4.0, no gating, 28 GB -- obtainable, licence compatible with research use; note 60 fps, so it checks the sliding/pendulum pipeline, not 240 fps bounce readout.

GPU budget: CoTracker3 on 1,200-2,400 trimmed clips at ~250 frames is of order 20-40 GPU-hours; batched tape fits at 1.5 s per forward+backward x ~50 iterations x ~1,000 non-sphere clips is ~20 GPU-hours; both fit <= 2 A6000s (GPUs 1-5 were idle at check time, nvidia-smi).

Hidden dependency the plan omits: the non-sphere per-clip fit of (alpha, mu, landing orientation) compares a 3-D rollout to 2-D tracks, which needs phone intrinsics and the camera-to-board extrinsics (a chessboard calibration day plus a scaled-orthographic or pinhole projector; src/render/camera.py has the pinhole but no real-camera calibration path). Spheres need none of this (e is scale-free; impact speed = g * fall time).

Hidden dependency in the audio route: e_t from inter-impact intervals needs three audible impacts; for the dead Physics 101 classes (cardboard e_h ~0.05-0.2 on glass/metal per p3 summary, foam 0.08-0.2) the second rebound is 0.1-0.6 cm from 0.15 m and may not click, so the two-route instrument gate can only be passed on bouncy spheres and the atlas's dead-material rows will be single-route.

Phone optics: at 3.0 m/s and 240 fps the object moves 12.5 mm per frame; iPhone native slo-mo gives no manual shutter (auto typically ~1/480 s -> ~6 mm blur), a third-party app or bright LEDs is needed for the stated 1/2000 s; rolling-shutter skew across a 7 cm object at 1080p240 is ~2 mm -- a bias, not a blocker, and constant in the parabola fit.

Schedule: 2,400 hand drops at ~30 s each is ~20 hands-on hours plus trimming; 240 fps 1080p clips are ~50 MB per 5 s -> ~120 GB raw. Feasible for one person in 3-4 capture days only with automatic trimming (audio click or motion onset) and object acquisition done before week 3.
verdicts.surviving_form: The plan survives but must be narrowed: (1) Run all gradient fits at the tilt rig's 420 substeps (1.5 s/clip) and restrict the differentiable part to flat-landed blocks and the bouncy/mid-damping regime, with the CEM fallback pre-committed for edge landings and dead materials, where the tape already drifts 10-17% from FD and flips sign at coarse steps; (2) treat the audio route as available only for e >~ 0.3 and state the instrument gate on bouncy spheres, reporting dead materials as single-route e_h with repeat IQR; (3) add a camera-calibration day (chessboard intrinsics + board extrinsics) before week 6, since the non-sphere 2-D-to-3-D fit depends on it and it is not in the 90-day plan; (4) the two-week first experiment is only feasible if the phone, tripod, lights and 10 objects are in hand on day 1 and p3 is ported to trimmed 250-frame clips in week 1 -- otherwise it slips by a week; (5) IRIS is 60 fps, so cite it as a sliding/pendulum pipeline check, not a bounce check.
verdicts.summary: Nothing in the plan depends on something that does not exist or cannot be obtained: the tape-safe exact-mesh DiffMeshScene is real and I verified today that its gradient through a single plane IMPACT matches finite differences (ratio 0.999-1.00 flat, up to 1.17 on an edge landing, 1.5 s and 0.4 GB per clip at tilt-rig substeps), the alpha knob is already a scalar map onto the differentiable cd, the p3 two-route tracker exists and failed only on frame rate, IRIS exists under CC-BY-NC, and the GPU budget (tens of GPU-hours) fits two shared A6000s. The 90-day milestone is reachable for spheres and flat-landing blocks; the risks are schedule and scope rather than existence: the unplanned camera calibration for the non-sphere 3-D fit, the audio route going silent for dead materials (which are most of the Physics 101 classes), the tape's sign flip at coarse steps and high damping, and the sheer hands-on capture load for one researcher. Not refuted; the gradient story shrinks to the regime measured here unless the edge-landing tape error is fixed.

verdicts.lens: Impact and practicality: who consumes the result, is the effect size actionable, does it answer the user's ask (differentiable physics, practical robot/sim system, scale beyond rooms)
evidence: The ask was 'actionable, differentiable physics engine, practical system for robots or simulations, very large scale beyond rooms, interactable worlds at scale'. The proposal self-reports against all three: 'differentiable_physics_role: For spheres: zero', 'scale_claim: Not rooms', 'On its own this is a dataset + calibration paper', 'policy-transfer value is untested'. It is an honest measurement project, not the direction requested.

The alpha table has exactly one consumer: this repo's own penalty kernel. src/sim/mesh_contact.py line 37 'HC = 1.0' and line 101 'fn = wp.max(k[b]*w*pen - HC*cde*w*pen*vnorm, 0.0)' is a custom Hunt-Crossley law; src/sim/rigs.py line 22 'TILT_RIG = {..., "alpha": 0.4}' is the only place alpha is read. Newton's shipped solvers (MuJoCo-Warp solref/solimp, XPBD, VBD, Featherstone) take no alpha; MuJoCo has no restitution coefficient at all; PhysX takes a scalar e with combine modes. 'Newton/Warp users get a measured alpha' is therefore false outside this project; only the alpha->e(v) mapping is portable, and PhysX users already fill e from handbook tables and randomize over it.

The project's own SimReady export already writes a scalar: src/simready/usd_physics.py line 31 'api.CreateRestitutionAttr(float(vals["restitution"]))' with 'provenance, confidence' fields. A measured e replaces a guessed e in one attribute per asset; no downstream test in the repo or in the proposal reads that attribute back, so the effect on any consumer is unmeasured and the proposal does not plan to measure it.

Robot pipelines do not hinge on e to +/-0.02: manipulation sim2real (pushing, grasping, in-hand) treats restitution as a domain-randomization range and is dominated by friction, mass and contact stiffness; nothing a manipulator does bounces an object. The proposal names no robot task and concedes the policy-transfer value is untested, so the 'practical for robots' box is empty.

The internal consumer is weak too: the stated use is 're-run the bounce/settle probes on the 13 assets with measured alpha', but CLAUDE.md records that the settle probe is 'dead as a magnitude' (<=1.29x), that the O-track video readouts (o10/o12/o13/o14) are retired, and that at the tilt rig 'landing changed' is the only visible consequence of alpha (vase rebounds once at 0.24 m/s instead of 0.72). Replacing 0.4 by a measured 0.3 or 0.6 changes a landing nobody reads.

Restitution is a PAIR property, which the project already found for friction ('one anchor is unavoidable', p5) and which Bounce-and-Learn (1904.06827) already showed for bounces: the surface dominates. A wooden board on a table/tripod is itself a vibrating plate; its thickness and support set the dissipation and are not modelled by the rigid plane in DiffMeshScene. The atlas rows would be 'object x this board', not 'material', so the catalogue column (PhysXNet/UniPhys material strings) inherits an unstated surface anchor and is not portable in the sense claimed.

The 'law vs parameter' diagnosis for GAUGE (2608.05948) would be made on the project's custom kernel, not on the stock Newton solvers GAUGE measured; p7 already answered the stock-solver half internally (tilt rig e = 0.77-1.00 over a 600x cd range: stiffness-dominated). Newton developers would not act on a calibration of a kernel they do not ship.

Venue fit: 1,200-2,400 phone clips at +/-0.02 e, compared against ContactNets/Dojo/DiffMJX (148 Hz AprilTags, per-object contact parameters), IRIS (2603.16432, instrument GT, 10 repeats) and PhysVid (2510.02311). A D&B or CoRL reviewer's first question is 'what task does this enable', and the proposal answers 'none tested'. Coefficient-of-restitution tables for many materials and balls already exist in engineering handbooks, sports-equipment standards and the physics-education literature (e.g. Cross, Am. J. Phys. 1999), so 'the first multi-material restitution table' is first only in the narrow sense of everyday objects with repeat IQR. Realistic ceiling: workshop / Scientific Data / internal calibration note.

What survives this lens: the headline IS falsifiable and the kill tests are concrete and pre-registered (instrument gate |e_h - e_t| < 0.05, g spread < 5%; one alpha across 2x speed within repeat IQR for >=10/15 materials; non-sphere CV < 15%). That is better than most proposals, but a falsifiable incremental number is still an incremental number.
verdicts.surviving_form: Demote it from a project to a 2-3 week instrument task inside a larger programme: (1) 10 spheres x 10 drops at 240 fps with the two-route check, run first on IRIS's dropping-ball videos against instrument GT, to establish 'a phone + CoTracker3 is a calibrated instrument' -- that validated pipeline is the reusable asset, usable afterwards for the measurements that do matter (friction/mass of many objects, held-out validation of catalogue assignments at scale); (2) replace the assumed alpha = 0.4 in src/sim/rigs.py with a measured value per surface class and record it; (3) ship the e rows only as one column of a larger validated sim-ready assignment paper (Proposal 1), with the surface anchor stated per row and no 'material restitution' claim. Drop the non-spherical gradient inversion, the GAUGE law-vs-parameter diagnosis and the standalone atlas paper: none has a consumer who would change a decision on the result.
verdicts.summary: Through the impact/practicality lens the proposal is refuted: it is a well-designed, falsifiable, pre-registered measurement exercise whose output -- restitution of ~50 household objects on one board to +/-0.02, plus a Hunt-Crossley alpha -- is consumed by exactly one piece of code (this repo's custom penalty kernel, HC=1.0 in mesh_contact.py, alpha in rigs.py) and by nothing a robot or a third-party simulator does. Newton's shipped solvers take no alpha, MuJoCo has no restitution, PhysX users already have handbook e and randomize over it, manipulation sim2real is insensitive to e, and the repo's own restitution consumers (settle probe, video readouts) are dead or retired. Restitution is a pair property dominated by the surface (Bounce-and-Learn), so the 'material' rows carry an unstated board anchor. The proposal concedes the user's three asks -- differentiable physics (zero for spheres), robot practicality (untested), scale beyond rooms (not rooms) -- and would land at workshop / Scientific Data level, not a top venue. Score 3/10: keep the phone-instrument gate and the measured alpha as a short internal calibration step; do not build the direction on it.

proposals.title: The Material Ledger: a measured, held-out-validated physics layer under sim-ready libraries, with one-slide surface transfer and an audit of the numbers the big libraries ship
proposals.thesis: For a one-person team the scale that matters in interactable worlds is materials and surfaces, not scenes: a table of friction, build-aware density and restitution measured from real motion with repeated-trial uncertainty, assigned through an LLM that only names the material, is the scale-free layer that every sim-ready pipeline (PhysX-3D/Anything/Omni, UniPhysGen, UrbanVerse-100K, MolmoSpaces, BEHAVIOR-1K, the SimReady spec) lacks, and the only one that can be validated against the real motion of held-out objects. We claim that this table, extended to a new surface by a single reference slide, predicts the real slides of never-seen objects on never-measured surfaces within 1.5x of a per-object oracle, while the VLM-assigned numbers those libraries ship predict the same real motion about 3x worse.
proposals.what_we_build: (1) The ledger: one row per material with mu_pair against the Physics 101 board (n trials, IQR, Laplace sigma), build-aware effective density (areal for hollow cardboard, solid, shell) and restitution alpha where measured, every value tagged measured / inferred / default; seeded from p1/p2/p5 (11 materials with kinetic mu, 3 bounded as never-sliding, 15 densities) and extended by phone capture. (2) The surface-anchor protocol: a new surface enters the ledger with one reference object (a ledger cardboard cube) slid 5 times at one angle; its ratio to the board row rescales every other row, which is the factorisation p5 measured on real data (ratio 0.75-1.05 across block-like materials) turned into a procedure. (3) The assignment tool: mesh + photo -> LLM names the material and build type (80% accurate in e1) -> ledger lookup -> SimReady USD with density, static/dynamic friction, restitution, CoM and inertia by build, plus provenance attributes, extending src/simready/usd_physics.py; with a stated mapping from our geometric-mean pair rule and Hunt-Crossley alpha onto PhysX's combine modes and restitution scalar. (4) The audit: each library's own assignment rule (UrbanVerse's GPT-4.1-from-renders, MolmoSpaces' GPT-4o mass, BEHAVIOR-1K's material-to-friction lookup, PhysXNet's VLM density, SimReady defaults), downloaded where the metadata is public and replicated from the published prompt otherwise, applied to the 101 Physics 101 objects and scored on their real slides with e1's harness, giving each library a real-motion error it has never reported. (5) e1-bench: that harness as a release, so any assignment function f(image, mesh) -> (mu, rho) receives a trajectory error on 359 real trials and a stays-or-slides accuracy on 198 cases.
proposals.builds_on_our_assets: scripts/e1_heldout.py (held-out protocol, cached LLM material naming, trajectory and outcome scoring); scripts/p1_ramp_friction.py and p2_ramp_all.py (643 tracked clips, slide/roll/stay classification, two-angle invariant, camera scale from object edges); scripts/p4_sim_loop.py (Newton reproduces real slides to 0.4-1.0 mm, simulator-fitted mu = analytic mu to 0.005); scripts/p5_transfer.py (anchor rule mu_body = mu_pair^2/0.45, factorisation ratio, areal/solid/shell mass transfer); docs/results/p101_density.json, p2_ramp_all.json, e1_heldout.json; src/track/cotracker.py (CoTracker3 at a 19 px grid); src/sim/mesh_scene.py (MeshProbeScene with mass_model and seat_on_plane) and src/sim/rigs.py (TILT_RIG with alpha); src/simready/usd_physics.py and scripts/write_full_simready.py (USD export with per-value provenance, already written); the f14/e1 LLM gateway (Claude, GPT, Gemini); scripts/g0_grad_check.py::DiffMeshScene for per-trial curvature; data/phys101 (4.5 GB on disk). Nothing from the judge, surprise, FPT, MYRIAD or Wan tracks is reused except as cited negatives.
proposals.differentiable_physics_role: Little, and that should be said plainly: the headline stands on mu sweeps through Newton with release-time and offset alignment (p4), which already match the analytic law to 0.005. Gradients through the verified object-on-surface path (g0: d(slide)/d(mu) by tape -0.5448 against -0.5453 by central finite differences) buy two second-order things: a Laplace sigma(mu) per trial from the tape's curvature, so every ledger row carries an uncertainty that does not depend on having ten repeats; and a joint fit of the nuisance parameters that dominate the error (the per-session ramp angle, where 1 deg moves mu by 0.02, plus per-trial release time and offset, about 200 parameters over a 93-trial session) by the trust-region Levenberg-Marquardt in src/optimize/lm.py, which nested sweeps handle badly. No multi-body gradients are needed, which matters because g0b/g0c showed that gradients through sustained body-body contact are not usable today. If the tape were unavailable the proposal would survive on sweeps and bootstrap IQRs.
proposals.scale_claim: The user's 'beyond rooms' framing is the wrong axis for one researcher: scene scale is where NVIDIA (NuRec, Isaac, SimReady packs), DeepMind (Genie) and UrbanVerse/MolmoSpaces already operate, and in all of them the physics is a VLM-guessed or artist-dialled layer that nobody validates. The actionable scale is the layer itself, which costs O(materials + surfaces), not O(objects x scenes).
